points.t: Burning (not itchy) vesicles or linear “kissing” plaques on exposed skin within about 24–48 h of outdoor night-time exposure or travel.
Vesicant contact dermatitis from beetle haemolymph — cantharidin (Meloidae) or paederin (Paederus) — causing intraepidermal blistering without a bite.
Flick the beetle off, wash with soap and water, cool compresses, short topical steroid; leave small blisters intact.
Eye involvement → same-day ophthalmology. Ingestion of cantharidin → A&E / TOXBASE.

points: Cantharidin breaks desmosomes → acantholysis and an intraepidermal blister with little dermal inflammation (usually no scarring). The same mechanism is used therapeutically on warts and molluscum.
Paederin from crushed *Paederus* beetles causes delayed linear erythema then vesicles/pustules.
**Ingesting** cantharidin (e.g. as a purported aphrodisiac) is systemically toxic — a medical emergency, not a skin problem.
Onset within hours to about 24–48 h; the patient often does not link the insect.
Vesicles/bullae on an erythematous base — often **linear or bizarre** where the beetle was wiped; “kissing” lesions in flexures favour Paederus.
Exposed sites: face, neck, arms, lower legs; toxin can be finger-transferred to eyes or genitals.
Heals in about a week, sometimes with lasting pigmentation in skin of colour.

cards.name: Paederus vs blister beetle
cards.clue: Both crush toxins; Paederus more linear/kissing/pustular; Meloidae more cantharidin bullae

cards.name: Phytophotodermatitis
cards.clue: Plant juice + sun; drip pattern; marked later pigmentation

items.t: Eye pain, redness, photophobia or reduced vision → irrigate and **same-day eye casualty**.
Extensive blistering, genital involvement, severe pain or systemic illness.
Returned traveller with fever — think beyond beetle dermatitis.

pearls.t: Ask “Did it **burn** or itch?” Burning linear blisters after lights outdoors → beetle; itchy grouped papules → bites.
Prevention: nets, screens, cover skin, shake bedding; never crush beetles on skin.
Teaching: quiz images of linear kissing lesions are usually **Paederus**, not Meloidae — but first aid is the same.
